title: Consensus Rules
subtitle: Who decides what a name resolves to?
intro: There are two hard problems in programming: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors. NoDNS doesn't try to solve naming for the whole world. It provides a framework where different consensus rules can coexist. The question 'who owns this domain?' has different answers depending on which consensus rule you follow. Nothing described here is production. Everything is a thought experiment.

principle.statement: NoDNS will never create a token. Naming is a utility, not an investment.

payments.anti_spam: Sats burned to miners (proof of work equivalent, no beneficiary)
payments.namespace_lease: Sats paid to the parent domain operator for subletting their namespace
payments.never: No token sale, no governance token, no staking, no ICO. If someone creates a $NODNS token, it's a scam.

models.name: Traditional DNS
models.description: The existing DNS system. You register a domain through a registrar, who leases it from a registry, who operates under ICANN's authority. A court order can seize your domain. A registrar can refuse to renew. Someone above you always has power over your name. This is what everyone uses today and it works fine for most things.
pros: Universal resolution — every device speaks DNS
Human-readable names
Well-understood legal framework
cons: Censorship-vulnerable — any level of the hierarchy can override
Lease, not ownership — you rent, never own
No cryptographic proof of ownership
Payment goes to intermediaries
models.resolution: DNS query → recursive resolver → authoritative nameserver → records

models.name: Tor .onion Addresses
models.authority: Cryptographic (derived from public key, same as .nostr)
models.description: Tor onion addresses are derived from a public key. Nobody can take your .onion address because nobody can derive a different key that produces the same address. This is the closest existing analogy to $npub.nostr — your key IS your address. The difference: .onion addresses route traffic through the Tor network, while $npub.nostr resolves to DNS records. Both share the same core insight: cryptographic identity as naming.
pros: Zero ambiguity — cryptographic proof of ownership
No squatting possible — you can't derive someone else's key
Free to claim (your keypair already exists)
No parent domain, no operator — just you and your key
cons: Not human-readable (56-char base32 strings)
Requires Tor Browser or special software
The .onion TLD only exists within the Tor network
No path to standard DNS resolution
models.resolution: Tor client → .onion address → rendezvous with hidden service
models.philosophy: The architectural predecessor to $npub.nostr. Same idea — your key is your identity — but for routing, not naming. $npub.nostr applies this insight to DNS: instead of routing packets, it resolves names.

models.name: $npub.nostr
models.authority: Cryptographic (nsec/npub — your keypair IS your domain credential)

reference.title: nodns-nameserver by Arjen
reference.description: Go implementation. JIT DNS server with embedded Khatru relay. Supports 17 DNS record types. Resolves *.nostr via Nostr subscriptions.

models.description: The purest consensus rule: your public key is your domain under .nostr. Nobody can take it from you because nobody can forge your signature. Nobody can squat someone else's public key because they can't produce valid events for it. The wire format (kind 11111 record tags) is zone-agnostic — the same event applies to .nostr, .nodns.shop, or any zone. Resolution is an infrastructure-layer concern, not a protocol-layer concern. Only $npub.nostr is supported — $string.nostr returns NXDOMAIN because there is no consensus mechanism for string ownership under .nostr.
models.wire_compat: The kind 11111 record tag ["record", "A", "", "1.2.3.4", ...] contains no zone information. The same event that creates records under .nostr also creates records under .nodns.shop. Zone operators choose which events to process by running a bot with their zone config.
pros: Zero ambiguity — cryptographic proof of ownership
No squatting possible — you can't fake someone's npub
Free to claim (your keypair already exists)
No parent domain, no operator — just you and your key
17 DNS record types supported
Zone-agnostic wire format — same events work everywhere
cons: Not human-readable (npubs are long strings)
Requires installing a local resolver or using DoH — not resolvable by standard DNS out of the box
The .nostr TLD only exists for people using a NoDNS resolver or DoH endpoint
$string.nostr is not supported — NXDOMAIN
models.resolution: Local DNS server (nodns-ns) or DoH endpoint → subscribes to Nostr relays → serves from cache
models.philosophy: The only consensus rule that is purely mathematical. No social contracts, no reputation, no economics, no operator. Just: do you have the private key? Then it's yours.

models.name: $npub.{parent_domain}
models.tagline: Private key decides, parent domain caches
models.authority: Cryptographic (nsec/npub) + parent domain operator mirrors to standard DNS
models.ownership_model: Inalienable mathematical ownership with optional DNS caching
models.description: The same rule as $npub.nostr, but under an existing parent domain. Your npub IS your subdomain. The parent domain operator runs a bot that subscribes to Nostr relays and pushes records to standard DNS via DDNS. This means anyone can resolve it with normal DNS — no special software needed. The operator can be paid to cache/mirror your records, but the Nostr events are the source of truth. This is a land grab: the parent domain operator is placing a new consensus rule above their own authority. The same zone-agnostic events that create records under .nostr also create records here — no wire format changes needed.
pros: Cryptographic proof of ownership (same as $npub.nostr)
No squatting possible
Resolves via standard DNS — every device can use it
Dual resolution: DNS and Nostr give identical results
If DNS is tampered with (MITM), the correct result is still available via Nostr
3-5 second propagation globally
Zone-agnostic events — same event works under any zone
cons: Not human-readable (npubs are long strings)
Parent domain operator must opt-in to this consensus rule
This IS a land grab — most TLDs won't like it because there is now an alternative rule above their authority
models.resolution: Nostr event (kind 11111) → signature verification → bot pushes to DNS via DDNS

dual_resolution.dns: Standard DNS query → zone's nameserver → records
dual_resolution.nostr: Nostr relay subscription → event verification → records
dual_resolution.conflict: Nostr always wins. If DNS returns different records than Nostr events, someone is tampering with DNS (MITM) or a court has ordered changes. The Nostr events remain the cryptographic truth.

models.philosophy: Your private key decides. The registrar can be paid to cache your records in standard DNS, but they cannot take your name because they cannot forge your signature. The parent domain operator sublets their namespace to cryptographic truth. Note: nodns.shop is a temporary backwards-compatibility convenience. If the domain is lost, the same events resolve under .nostr or any other zone running a NoDNS bot. The domain is not the protocol.

models.name: $string.{parent_domain}
models.tagline: Parent domain delegates authority to a private key
models.authority: Delegation from parent domain owner (via signed Nostr event)
models.description: An existing domain owner delegates a human-readable name to a specific npub for a fixed duration. The delegation is a signed Nostr event — irrevocable within the validity period. The operator is subletting their namespace. They choose to recognize Nostr events as the authority for their zone. Payment goes to the parent domain operator as a lease of their namespace. Censorship-resistant at the Nostr layer (delegation event can't be forged), but a court can order the operator to change DNS records.
pros: Human-readable names
Delegation is verifiable on Nostr (public audit trail)
Price locked at registration time
Dual resolution — same records via DNS and Nostr
Censorship-resistant at the Nostr layer (delegation event can't be forged)
cons: Trust in operator — they could theoretically re-delegate (reputation risk)
Lease duration bounded by operator's own domain registration
Court can order operator to change DNS records (but Nostr events remain)
Social censorship resistance, not cryptographic
models.resolution: Delegation event on Nostr → npub publishes records → bot mirrors events to DNS

dual_resolution.dns: Standard DNS query → zone's nameserver → records
dual_resolution.nostr: Nostr relay → delegation event + record events → verify signatures → records
dual_resolution.conflict: Nostr events are the truth. DNS is a cache. If they disagree, DNS has been tampered with.

models.philosophy: The operator sublets their namespace. They choose to recognize Nostr events as the authority. A TLD operator could run their own nodns-bot and offer this to all their registrants. The payment is a lease of namespace, not a token.

models.name: $string.pob
models.tagline: Burn sats to claim a namespace
models.description: A speculative consensus rule where you prove you burned Bitcoin (sending sats to unspendable addresses, contributing to Bitcoin's security) to claim a namespace. Based on ThomasV's proof-of-burn model for Nostr namespaces. The idea: burning is costly, so names have implicit economic weight. No token is created — sats go to miners.
pros: No token created — sats go to miners (net positive for Bitcoin security)
Economic cost prevents trivial spam
Trustless — the burn proof is on-chain
cons: Deep pockets problem — anyone with more sats can out-burn you and take your name
How do you prevent typosquatting by burning tiny amounts?
Ownership change mechanism unclear — does highest burner always win?
Someone with deep pockets wanting to sabotage you can keep burning
Operator gets no revenue (sats burned, not paid to operator)
open_questions: Should there be an exponential burn curve to make takeovers progressively more expensive?
What happens to the namespace if nobody is burning to maintain it?
How to handle disputes — first burner or highest burner?
Could this work as a commit-reveal scheme to prevent front-running?
models.philosophy: Philosophically elegant — you prove commitment by destroying value. But the economics create attack vectors that may make it unusable in practice.

models.name: $string.wot
models.tagline: Your social circle decides what the name resolves to
models.authority: Social graph (who you trust determines resolution)
models.description: A highly experimental model where a name resolves differently depending on which social circle you belong to. Much like how 'the pub' means different places to different people depending on their context, a WoT domain resolves based on who you trust. Your web of trust defines your namespace. Not yet explored in depth.
pros: No central authority at all — resolution is subjective
Inherently censorship-resistant (there's nothing to censor — everyone sees different results)
Reflects how naming actually works in real life (context-dependent)
cons: No universal resolution — different people see different results
This might make it useless for DNS (DNS assumes global consistency)
Complex to implement (social graph traversal, trust scoring)
Susceptible to Sybil attacks and trust manipulation
open_questions: How to bootstrap trust without centralization?
Can this coexist with DNS, or is it fundamentally incompatible?
What's the user experience? 'alice.wot resolves to... depends on who you ask'?
models.philosophy: The most radical model. It acknowledges that naming is fundamentally social and context-dependent. 'The pub' means different things to different people — and that's fine. But it may not be DNS.

models.name: $string.eburn
models.tagline: Exponentially increasing cost to take over a name
models.description: A variant of Proof of Burn where the cost to take over an existing name increases exponentially. If you burned 1000 sats to claim 'alice.eburn', someone else would need to burn 10,000 to take it. Then you'd need 100,000 to reclaim it. The exponential curve makes it prohibitively expensive to dislodge a legitimate owner. Not yet explored in depth.
pros: Strong protection against deep-pocket takeovers (exponential defense)
Legitimate owners can defend with smaller amounts
Still no token — sats burned to miners
cons: Exponential curves can reach absurd numbers quickly
Doesn't solve the problem — just delays it
Names become de facto permanent after a few cycles
Complex to reason about economically
open_questions: Should the exponential reset after a period of inactivity?
How does this interact with genuine ownership disputes?
models.philosophy: Takes the PoB model and adds a defense-in-depth mechanism. But the complexity may not be worth it.

models.name: Crypto Naming Tokens
models.description: Various projects have created naming systems backed by blockchain tokens. You buy a name, you get a token that represents ownership. The smart contract or chain consensus enforces who controls the name. NoDNS takes a different path: no token, no blockchain. Included for comparison — NoDNS explicitly rejects this approach.
pros: Censorship-resistant (smart contract can't be court-ordered)
Transferable property (you can sell the token)
Programmable (subdomains, records as smart contract state)
cons: Creates a token economy around naming — financial speculation distorts the namespace
Requires blockchain infrastructure to resolve
Gas fees for updates
Bifurcated resolution — normal DNS doesn't see these names without special software
models.resolution: Special resolver / browser extension → blockchain RPC → contract state → records

closing.title: What all of these have in common
closing.body: Every model above is just a different consensus rule — a different social contract about what 'looking up a name' means. Traditional DNS says 'the registrar decides.' ENS says 'the smart contract decides.' NoDNS says 'the private key decides, and the parent domain operator can be paid to cache.' Proof of Burn says 'economic commitment decides.' Web of Trust says 'your community decides.' They're all trying to answer the same question: when someone types a name into their browser, who gets to say what it resolves to?
closing.no_token: NoDNS will never create a token. Any payment is either burned as anti-spam or paid to the parent domain operator as a lease of their namespace.
closing.research: Researching other name resolution methods beyond what's listed here is an open TODO. If you have ideas, open an issue.
closing.nothing_is_production: Nothing described here is production. The protocol is an experimental draft. The proof-of-concept is live at nodns.shop. Everything else is a thought experiment.
